Build a value scale

A photograph with neutral lighting is essential. Yellow room light, filters and harsh shadows push skin toward colors that belong to the photo rather than necessarily to the person.

Work with concrete measurements and references. Counting stitches, centimeters, strands or weight reveals incompatibilities that an inspiration photo cannot show. Decide how many shades you need

For a small face, three to five well-ordered shades can work better than twelve near-identical ones. Portrait resolution determines how many steps can be shown without creating confetti.

Think about how the piece will be used after finishing. A framed picture, washable accessory and object handled every day need very different assembly decisions. Control undertones and transitions

Check the palette in grayscale: highlights should remain lighter and shadows darker. Then evaluate warm, cool, reddish or olive undertones within that value structure.

Do not add complexity simply because it is possible. More colors, layers or tools do not improve a project unless they visibly change readability, durability or comfort. Avoid universal recipes

Avoid one universal recipe for every person. Two portraits with similar lightness may need different color families to preserve likeness and avoid an artificial result.

If a problem appears, change one variable at a time and record what you do. That discipline reveals the actual cause and prevents a small repair from becoming several simultaneous changes.
